q: One end of a long horizontal rope is moved steadily up and down, and a wave travels along the rope. How do the particles of the rope move?
o: Up and down about their mean positions
Along the rope together with the wave
In circles around the axis of the rope
Back and forth along the length of the rope
x: The particles of the rope vibrate up and down about their mean positions while the disturbance travels along the rope. They do not travel with the wave.

q: A long spring (slinky) lying on a smooth table is pushed and pulled repeatedly along its length at one end. The wave produced consists of:
o: Crests and troughs moving along the spring
Coils moving permanently towards the far end
Compressions and rarefactions moving along the spring
A single pulse that stays at the hand
x: Pushing and pulling along the length bunches the coils together (compressions) and spreads them apart (rarefactions); these regions travel along the spring as a longitudinal wave. Crests and troughs belong to transverse waves.

q: A single sharp up-and-down jerk is given to one end of a stretched rope. What is produced?
o: A pulse that travels along the rope
A stationary wave with fixed nodes
A longitudinal wave along the rope
x: A single disturbance produces a single pulse that moves along the rope. A continuous periodic wave needs the end to be moved up and down continuously.

q: A small ribbon is tied to the middle of a long stretched rope. As a transverse wave passes along the rope, the ribbon:
o: Moves along the rope to the far end
Vibrates up and down but stays at the same place along the rope
Moves back towards the hand that is shaking the rope
x: The ribbon moves with the rope particle it is tied to, which only vibrates about its mean position. The wave passes on, but the ribbon does not travel along the rope.

q: A student shakes the end of a stretched rope with a larger up-and-down movement of the hand, keeping the rate of shaking the same. Which property of the wave increases?
x: A bigger movement of the source gives a bigger maximum displacement, i.e. a larger amplitude. Frequency is set by the rate of shaking and speed by the rope, so the wavelength does not change either.

q: A student shakes a stretched rope up and down twice as often per second, without changing the tension in the rope. Which statement about the new wave is correct?
o: Its speed doubles and its wavelength stays the same
Its wavelength halves and its speed stays the same
Its frequency and wavelength both double
Its speed and frequency both halve
x: The wave speed depends on the rope and its tension, so it stays the same. Since v = fλ, doubling f halves λ.

q: One end of a slinky spring lying on a table is moved quickly from side to side, across the length of the spring. The wave produced is:
o: Longitudinal, because the coils move perpendicular to the direction of travel
Transverse, because the coils move parallel to the direction of travel
Longitudinal, because the coils move parallel to the direction of travel
Transverse, because the coils move perpendicular to the direction of travel
x: Moving the end sideways makes the coils vibrate at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels, so the wave is transverse. A slinky gives a longitudinal wave only when pushed and pulled along its length.

q: In a progressive wave travelling along a rope, how does the motion of each particle compare with that of the particle just before it (nearer the source)?
o: It is exactly the same and exactly in step
It is the same vibration, but starts slightly later
x: Each particle repeats the vibration of the particle before it, with a small time delay. This delay from particle to particle is what makes the disturbance travel along the rope.

q: Which statement about waves in ropes and springs is correct?
o: A wave is produced by a disturbance or vibration at the source
A wave can travel only if the whole rope moves forward
A wave on a rope can only be longitudinal
A wave on a slinky spring can only be transverse
x: A wave starts from a disturbance at the source that is passed on through the medium. A rope carries transverse waves, while a slinky can carry both transverse and longitudinal waves.

q: Which of the following needs a material medium to travel?
x: Sound is a mechanical wave, so it needs a medium. Light, radio waves and X-rays are electromagnetic waves and can travel through a vacuum.

q: An electric bell rings inside a sealed glass jar. As the air is pumped out, the sound becomes fainter and fainter, but the bell can still be seen clearly. This shows that:
o: Sound needs a medium, but light does not
Light needs a medium, but sound does not
Both sound and light need a medium
Glass blocks sound but not light
x: The sound fades as the air (its medium) is removed, while light still passes through the near-vacuum. Glass does not block the sound, since the bell is heard clearly before the air is removed.

q: Light from huge explosions on the Sun reaches the Earth, but their sound never does. The reason is that:
o: The space between the Sun and the Earth is nearly a vacuum, and sound needs a medium
Sound travels too slowly to cover the distance
The Earth's atmosphere absorbs all sound coming from the Sun
Light waves are longitudinal while sound waves are transverse
x: Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot cross the near-vacuum of space, however long it has. Light is an electromagnetic wave and needs no medium.

q: Two astronauts standing close together on the Moon cannot hear each other speak directly, but they can talk by radio. Why?
o: Radio waves are mechanical waves that need no medium
Sound travels faster than radio waves on the Moon
The Moon has no atmosphere to carry sound, while radio waves can travel through a vacuum
The low gravity on the Moon stops sound waves
x: There is no air on the Moon, so sound (a mechanical wave) cannot travel between them. Radio waves are electromagnetic and travel through a vacuum.

q: Electromagnetic waves consist of:
o: Vibrations of the atoms of the source only
x: An electromagnetic wave is made of oscillating electric and magnetic fields, which need no particles to carry them. That is why such waves can travel through a vacuum.

q: Which of the following is a mechanical wave?
o: Waves on the surface of water
x: Water waves are carried by the water particles, so they are mechanical waves. Microwaves, infrared and ultraviolet are all parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.

q: Which statement is correct for all electromagnetic waves travelling in a vacuum?
o: They travel faster when their frequency is higher
They travel at the same speed, 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
They need a thin layer of air to travel
They all have the same wavelength
x: In a vacuum every electromagnetic wave travels at c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, whatever its frequency. Different frequencies have different wavelengths, since λ = c/f.

q: A wave from the Sun crosses the nearly empty space to the Earth, a distance of 1.5 × 10¹¹ m, in 500 s. What can be concluded about this wave?
o: It is a sound wave, since sound travels fastest in empty space
It is an electromagnetic wave, since it crosses a vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹
It is a mechanical wave carried by particles in space
It is a longitudinal wave, since it carries energy
x: Speed = 1.5 × 10¹¹ / 500 = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the speed of light, and it crosses a vacuum. Only an electromagnetic wave can do this; mechanical waves such as sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

q: Which of the following is NOT an electromagnetic wave?
x: Ultrasound is sound of frequency above 20 kHz, a mechanical wave that needs a medium. Gamma rays, visible light and radio waves are electromagnetic.

q: The amplitude of a wave is:
o: The maximum displacement of a particle from its mean position
The distance between two consecutive crests
The number of waves passing a point per second
The distance travelled by the wave in one second
x: Amplitude is the greatest displacement of a vibrating particle from its mean (rest) position. The distance between consecutive crests is the wavelength, and waves per second is the frequency.

q: For a transverse wave, the wavelength is the distance between:
o: A crest and the next trough
The mean position and a crest
Two neighbouring points of zero displacement
x: One wavelength is the distance between two consecutive crests (or troughs). A crest and the next trough, or two neighbouring zero-displacement points, are only half a wavelength apart.

q: In a longitudinal wave, the distance between the centre of a compression and the centre of the next rarefaction is 0.4 m. The wavelength is:
x: A compression and the next rarefaction are half a wavelength apart. So λ = 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 m.

q: A compression in a sound wave travelling through air is a region where:
o: The air particles are farthest apart and the pressure is low
The air particles remain permanently at rest
The air pressure is the same as in a rarefaction
The air particles are closest together and the pressure is high
x: In a compression the particles are crowded together, so density and pressure are higher than normal. A rarefaction is the opposite: particles spread apart and pressure lower.

q: A wave has a frequency of 50 Hz. Its time period is:
x: T = 1/f = 1/50 = 0.02 s. Period and frequency are reciprocals of each other.

q: The time period of a wave is the time taken for:
o: The wave to travel one metre
The amplitude to fall to half its value
One complete vibration of a particle of the medium
The wave to travel half a wavelength
x: The period is the time for one complete vibration of a particle. In this time the wave moves forward one full wavelength, not half.

q: Through what distance does a progressive wave move forward during one time period?
o: A distance equal to the amplitude
x: In one period each particle completes one vibration and the wave advances by one wavelength. This is why v = λ/T = fλ.

q: In a transverse wave, the displacement of a particle at a crest is +3 cm from the mean position. What is the displacement of a particle at a trough?
x: A trough is the point of maximum displacement on the opposite side of the mean position, so its displacement is −3 cm. The amplitude, 3 cm, is the same for crest and trough.

q: In a transverse wave, the vertical distance from the top of a crest to the bottom of a trough is 10 cm, and the horizontal distance from a crest to the next trough is 25 cm. The amplitude and wavelength are:
x: Crest-to-trough height is twice the amplitude, so amplitude = 5 cm. Crest to next trough is half a wavelength, so λ = 2 × 25 = 50 cm.

q: In the study of waves, the term 'medium' means:
o: The source that produces the vibration
The middle (mean) position of a vibrating particle
The substance through which the wave travels
The average of the highest and lowest wave speeds
x: The medium is the material, such as air, water, a rope or a spring, through which a mechanical wave travels. The middle position of a vibrating particle is called its mean position.

q: A sound wave of frequency 500 Hz has a wavelength of 0.68 m in air. Its speed is:
x: v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. Dividing instead of multiplying gives the wrong values.

q: Sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹ in air. What is the wavelength of a note of frequency 170 Hz?
x: λ = v/f = 340/170 = 2 m. Multiplying v by f gives the meaningless 57 800 m; f/v gives 0.5.

q: An FM radio station broadcasts at a frequency of 100 MHz. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, the wavelength of its waves is:
x: λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸)/(1 × 10⁸) = 3 m. Remember 1 MHz = 10⁶ Hz, so 100 MHz = 10⁸ Hz.

q: A wave has a time period of 0.02 s and a wavelength of 4 m. Its speed is:
x: v = λ/T = 4/0.02 = 200 m s⁻¹ (equivalently f = 50 Hz and v = 50 × 4). 50 is just the frequency, not the speed.

q: Water waves of wavelength 2 m pass a fixed post. If 30 complete waves pass the post in 10 s, what is the speed of the waves?
x: Frequency f = 30/10 = 3 Hz and λ = 2 m. So v = fλ = 3 × 2 = 6 m s⁻¹.

q: On a string carrying a transverse wave, a crest and the next trough are 0.5 m apart. If the frequency is 20 Hz, the wave speed is:
x: Crest to next trough is λ/2, so λ = 1 m. Then v = fλ = 20 × 1 = 20 m s⁻¹; taking λ = 0.5 m wrongly gives 10 m s⁻¹.

q: A sound of frequency 500 Hz passes from air, where its speed is 340 m s⁻¹, into water, where its speed is 1500 m s⁻¹. Its wavelength in water is:
x: The frequency does not change when a wave enters a new medium. In water λ = v/f = 1500/500 = 3 m; 0.68 m is its wavelength in air.

q: Waves travel through a medium at a constant speed. If the frequency of the waves is doubled, the wavelength:
x: From v = fλ with v fixed, λ is inversely proportional to f. Doubling f halves λ.

q: The human ear can hear frequencies from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. If sound travels at 340 m s⁻¹, the shortest wavelength a person can hear is:
x: The shortest wavelength belongs to the highest frequency: λ = 340/20 000 = 0.017 m = 1.7 cm. 17 m is the longest wavelength, at 20 Hz.

q: Microwaves used in a radar have a wavelength of 3 cm. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, their frequency is:
x: λ = 3 cm = 0.03 m, so f = c/λ = (3 × 10⁸)/0.03 = 10¹⁰ Hz. Forgetting to convert cm to m gives 10⁸ Hz.

q: A progressive wave transfers:
o: Matter from the source to the receiver
Energy from one place to another without net transfer of matter
Both energy and matter in the direction of travel
x: A progressive wave carries energy through the medium, while the particles of the medium only vibrate about their mean positions and are not carried along.

q: A cork floating on a pond bobs up and down as ripples pass it, but it does not move outward with the ripples. This shows that:
o: The water is flowing outward with the wave
The wave carries energy, while the water particles only vibrate about their positions
The cork is too heavy to be moved by any wave
x: The cork gains energy from the wave and so moves up and down, but like the water around it, it stays in place. Energy travels outward; the water does not.

q: The energy carried by a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude. If the amplitude is doubled while the frequency stays the same, the energy carried becomes:
x: Energy ∝ (amplitude)², so doubling the amplitude multiplies the energy by 2² = 4.

q: Two waves of the same frequency travel in the same medium. Their amplitudes are in the ratio 3 : 1. Given that wave energy is proportional to amplitude squared, the ratio of the energies they carry is:
x: Energy ∝ amplitude², so the ratio is 3² : 1² = 9 : 1.

q: How is energy passed along by a progressive mechanical wave?
o: Each vibrating particle passes energy on to the neighbouring particle
Particles near the source travel to the far end, carrying the energy
Energy jumps straight from source to receiver without using the medium
The medium heats up and the heat travels as the wave
x: Each particle, as it vibrates, pushes or pulls its neighbour and sets it vibrating, so energy is handed on from particle to particle. The particles themselves stay near their mean positions.

q: Loud music from a loudspeaker makes a sheet of paper held nearby vibrate. This is evidence that sound waves:
o: Carry air from the speaker to the paper
x: The paper starts vibrating because the sound wave delivers energy to it. The air itself is not carried from the speaker to the paper; its particles only vibrate.

q: Sunlight warms the Earth even though the space between the Sun and the Earth is almost empty. This shows that:
o: Heat reaches the Earth by conduction through space
Sound waves from the Sun carry the energy
Only mechanical waves can carry energy
Electromagnetic waves can transfer energy through a vacuum
x: Light and infrared are electromagnetic waves, which carry energy without needing a medium. Conduction and sound both need matter, which space lacks.

q: Which statement about a progressive wave is correct?
o: The particles of the medium travel along with the wave
Energy is carried in the direction in which the wave travels
Energy is trapped between fixed points and is not carried forward
The medium moves permanently away from the source
x: In a progressive wave energy flows forward in the direction of travel. Energy trapped between fixed points describes a stationary wave, not a progressive one.

q: Ripples spread out in circles from a stone dropped into a pond. Even if no energy were lost to friction, their amplitude would decrease as they move outward. This is because:
o: The same energy is spread over a larger and larger circle
The frequency of the ripples increases as they spread
The ripples speed up as they move outward
The water particles move outward and leave the wave
x: The energy of the wave is shared over an ever larger circumference, so the energy at each point falls. Since energy ∝ amplitude², the amplitude also falls.

q: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium vibrate:
o: Parallel to the direction of travel of the wave
Perpendicular to the direction of travel of the wave
In circles around the direction of travel
Only at the source and nowhere else
x: In a transverse wave particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of propagation, forming crests and troughs. Vibration parallel to the direction of travel describes a longitudinal wave.

q: Sound waves travelling through air are:
x: In air, sound travels as a series of compressions and rarefactions, with particles vibrating along the direction of travel, so it is longitudinal. Sound is mechanical and needs a medium.

q: Which pair are both features of a longitudinal wave?
x: A longitudinal wave is made of compressions (particles close together) and rarefactions (particles spread apart). Crests and troughs belong to transverse waves.

q: Which of the following is NOT a transverse wave?
o: A wave on a plucked guitar string
x: Sound in air is longitudinal. Light and radio waves are transverse electromagnetic waves, and a wave on a plucked string is a transverse mechanical wave.

q: Which property is shown only by transverse waves?
x: Polarisation means restricting the vibrations to one plane, which is possible only when vibrations are across the direction of travel. All waves, including longitudinal ones, can be reflected, refracted and diffracted.

q: Transverse mechanical waves cannot travel through the bulk of a gas, but longitudinal waves can. The reason is that a gas:
o: Cannot provide a restoring force when its layers are pushed sideways
Has particles that cannot move at all
Is a perfect insulator of heat
x: A transverse wave needs the medium to pull a displaced layer back sideways, which requires rigidity; a gas has none. A gas does resist being compressed, so longitudinal waves such as sound can pass.

q: Which statement is true for both transverse and longitudinal waves?
o: They consist of compressions and rarefactions
They transfer energy and obey v = fλ
Their particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel
x: Every progressive wave transfers energy and satisfies v = fλ. Polarisation and perpendicular vibration apply only to transverse waves; compressions and rarefactions only to longitudinal waves.

q: Through which of the following can longitudinal mechanical waves travel?
x: Longitudinal waves need only a medium that resists compression, which all solids, liquids and gases do. No mechanical wave can travel through a vacuum.

q: A wave along a stretched string is transverse, while sound in air is longitudinal. Which statement correctly compares them?
o: In the string wave crests travel, while in the sound wave crests and troughs of air travel
The string wave needs no medium, while sound needs a medium
In the string wave particles move across the direction of travel, while in sound they move along it
In the string wave particles move along the direction of travel, while in sound they move across it
x: String particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of travel; air particles in sound vibrate parallel to it. Both are mechanical waves and both need a medium.

q: Light passing through one polaroid filter can be cut off by turning a second polaroid placed after it. Sound cannot be blocked in this way. This shows that:
o: Light is longitudinal while sound is transverse
Light is a mechanical wave like sound
Light is transverse while sound is longitudinal
x: Only transverse waves can be polarised, so the polaroid effect shows light is transverse. Sound is not affected because its vibrations are along the direction of travel, i.e. it is longitudinal.

q: In which of the following does sound travel fastest?
x: Sound generally travels fastest in solids, then liquids, then gases. It cannot travel at all in a vacuum.

q: The speed of sound in a medium is given by v = √(E/ρ), where ρ is the density. Here E stands for:
o: The energy of the sound wave
The modulus of elasticity of the medium
x: Newton showed that the speed of sound depends on the elasticity (modulus E) and density ρ of the medium: v = √(E/ρ). It does not depend on the wave's energy or amplitude.

q: In deriving his formula for the speed of sound in air, Newton assumed that the compressions and rarefactions take place:
x: Newton assumed the temperature of the air stays constant as sound passes, i.e. an isothermal process. Laplace later corrected this to adiabatic.

q: According to Newton's formula, the speed of sound in a gas of pressure P and density ρ is:
x: Newton took the elastic modulus of a gas equal to its pressure, giving v = √(P/ρ). The formula with γ is Laplace's corrected version.

q: Newton took the elastic (bulk) modulus of air to be equal to its pressure P. Which law did he apply to get this result?
x: For an isothermal change Boyle's law (PV = constant) gives the bulk modulus E = P. The adiabatic law gives E = γP, which is Laplace's correction.

q: A gas has pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and density 1.6 kg m⁻³. Using Newton's formula, the speed of sound in it is:
x: v = √(P/ρ) = √(1.0 × 10⁵ / 1.6) = √62 500 = 250 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 62 500.

q: The bulk modulus of water is 2.25 × 10⁹ Pa and its density is 1000 kg m⁻³. Using v = √(E/ρ), the speed of sound in water is:
Steel is thousands of times denser than air, yet sound travels much faster in steel. Using v = √(E/ρ), the reason is that:
o: Steel is actually less dense than air
Sound in steel travels as an electromagnetic wave
The elasticity of steel exceeds that of air by a much bigger factor than its density does
The particles of steel are farther apart than those of air
x: Speed depends on the ratio E/ρ. The modulus of steel is enormously larger than that of air, far more than enough to outweigh its larger density, so E/ρ and hence v are much greater.

q: What is the SI unit of the quantity √(P/ρ), where P is pressure and ρ is density?
x: P/ρ has units (kg m⁻¹ s⁻²)/(kg m⁻³) = m² s⁻². Its square root has units m s⁻¹, as a speed must.

q: Two gases are at the same pressure. Their densities are ρ and 4ρ. According to Newton's formula, the ratio of the speed of sound in the less dense gas to that in the denser gas is:
x: At equal pressure v ∝ 1/√ρ. So v₁/v₂ = √(4ρ/ρ) = 2, a ratio of 2 : 1; the lighter gas carries sound faster.

q: In Laplace's formula for the speed of sound, v = √(γP/ρ), the symbol γ stands for:
o: The ratio of molar specific heats, Cv/Cp
The density of air at STP
The ratio of molar specific heats, Cp/Cv
x: γ = Cp/Cv, the ratio of the molar specific heat at constant pressure to that at constant volume. For air γ ≈ 1.4, which is greater than 1.

q: Laplace argued that sound travels through air adiabatically, not isothermally. His reason was that:
o: Compressions and rarefactions happen too quickly for heat exchange, and air is a poor conductor of heat
Air is a very good conductor of heat
The temperature of air stays exactly constant as sound passes
Sound waves always have very small amplitudes
x: The changes are so rapid, and air conducts heat so poorly, that heat cannot flow in or out of a compressed or rarefied region. Such a change is adiabatic.

q: In Laplace's treatment, the bulk modulus of air for the passage of sound is taken as:
x: For an adiabatic change PVᵞ = constant, which gives the bulk modulus E = γP. Newton's isothermal assumption gave E = P.

q: For the same gas under the same conditions, the ratio of the speed of sound given by Laplace's formula to that given by Newton's formula is:
x: v(Laplace)/v(Newton) = √(γP/ρ) / √(P/ρ) = √γ. Since γ > 1, Laplace's value is larger.

q: Newton's formula gives about 280 m s⁻¹ for the speed of sound in air at STP. With γ = 1.4 (√1.4 ≈ 1.18), Laplace's correction raises this to about:
x: v = 280 × √1.4 ≈ 280 × 1.18 ≈ 330 m s⁻¹, close to the measured value (about 332 m s⁻¹). Multiplying by 1.4 instead of √1.4 gives 392 m s⁻¹.

q: For a certain gas, Newton's formula gives the speed of sound as 250 m s⁻¹. If γ = 1.44 for this gas, the speed given by Laplace's formula is:
x: Laplace's value = Newton's value × √γ = 250 × √1.44 = 250 × 1.2 = 300 m s⁻¹. Using γ instead of √γ gives 360 m s⁻¹.

q: According to Laplace, as a sound wave passes through air, the temperature of the air:
o: Rises slightly in compressions and falls slightly in rarefactions
Falls in compressions and rises in rarefactions
Rises in both compressions and rarefactions
x: In an adiabatic compression the gas warms, and in an adiabatic expansion it cools. So compressions are slightly warmer and rarefactions slightly cooler than normal.

q: A gas has pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa, density 1.0 kg m⁻³ and γ = 1.6. Using Laplace's formula, the speed of sound in the gas is:
x: v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.6 × 10⁵ / 1.0) = √(16 × 10⁴) = 400 m s⁻¹. Leaving out γ (Newton's formula) gives about 316 m s⁻¹.

q: Which statement about Laplace's correction is correct?
o: It showed that sound travels through air isothermally
It reduced the speed calculated by Newton
It applies only to sound travelling in solids
It brought the calculated speed of sound in air into agreement with experiment
x: By treating the process as adiabatic, Laplace multiplied Newton's value by √γ, raising it from about 280 to about 332 m s⁻¹, close to the measured value.

q: How does the speed of sound in air depend on the temperature T of the air?
x: Since v = √(γP/ρ) and P/ρ is proportional to the absolute temperature, v ∝ √T with T in kelvin.

q: The speed of sound in air at 27 °C is v. At what temperature will it become 2v?
x: v ∝ √T, so doubling v needs T to become four times: 4 × 300 K = 1200 K = 927 °C. Giving 1200 °C forgets to convert back from kelvin.

q: The speed of sound in air is 332 m s⁻¹ at 0 °C and increases by 0.61 m s⁻¹ for each 1 °C rise in temperature. The speed of sound at 20 °C is:
The pressure of a sample of air is doubled while its temperature is kept constant. The speed of sound in it:
x: At constant temperature, doubling P also doubles the density ρ (Boyle's law), so P/ρ and hence v = √(γP/ρ) do not change.

q: At the same temperature and pressure, sound travels slightly faster in moist air than in dry air because:
o: Moist air is denser than dry air
Moist air is less dense than dry air
Water vapour has a higher boiling point than air
Moisture makes air a better conductor of heat
x: Water vapour is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen it replaces, so moist air has a lower density. Since v ∝ 1/√ρ, sound travels faster in it.

q: Hydrogen and oxygen are at the same temperature and pressure, and both have the same γ. The density of oxygen is 16 times that of hydrogen. The speed of sound in hydrogen is:
o: One quarter of that in oxygen
The same as that in oxygen
x: With the same γ and P, v ∝ 1/√ρ. So v(hydrogen)/v(oxygen) = √16 = 4.

q: Which change does NOT affect the speed of sound in air?
o: Raising the temperature of the air
Increasing the humidity of the air
Replacing the air by a lighter gas at the same pressure
Changing the frequency of the sound
x: The speed depends on the properties of the medium (temperature, density, humidity), not on the frequency of the source. A higher frequency simply gives a shorter wavelength at the same speed.

q: The speed of sound in air at 0 °C is 332 m s⁻¹. Taking √2 ≈ 1.41, the speed of sound in air at 273 °C is about:
x: The absolute temperature rises from 273 K to 546 K, i.e. doubles, so v increases by √2: 332 × 1.41 ≈ 469 m s⁻¹. Doubling the speed would need four times the absolute temperature.

q: A loud sound and a soft sound of the same pitch are produced at the same moment in still air. Compared with the soft sound, the loud sound travels:
o: Faster at first and then slower
x: The speed of sound depends on the medium, not on the amplitude (loudness) of the wave. Both sounds reach a listener at the same time.

q: Two sources of waves are said to be coherent when they have:
o: The same frequency and a constant phase difference
The same wavelength but a randomly changing phase
x: Coherent sources emit waves of the same frequency with a phase difference that stays constant in time. Only then does a steady interference pattern form.

q: Two loudspeakers are driven by two separate oscillators set to nominally the same frequency. A fixed pattern of loud and quiet points is not obtained because:
o: The phase difference between the two sources does not stay constant
The amplitudes of the two waves are always equal
x: Two independent oscillators are never exactly matched, so their phase difference keeps drifting. The sources are not coherent and the loud and quiet points keep moving.

q: Two coherent waves of amplitudes 3 mm and 5 mm arrive at a point exactly in phase. The amplitude of the resultant wave at that point is:
x: In phase, the displacements add at every instant, so the resultant amplitude is 3 + 5 = 8 mm. 2 mm would be the result for waves in opposite phase.

q: At a point of constructive interference between waves from two coherent sources:
o: A crest always falls on a trough
The two waves have different frequencies
A crest falls on a crest and a trough on a trough
The resultant displacement is always zero
x: Constructive interference means the waves arrive in phase: crest meets crest and trough meets trough, giving maximum amplitude. Crest on trough gives destructive interference.

q: Two coherent waves of equal amplitude meet in phase at a point. Compared with the intensity of one wave alone, the intensity at that point is:
x: The resultant amplitude is doubled, and intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so intensity becomes 2² = 4 times. Twice comes from forgetting to square.

q: For two waves of wavelength λ, a path difference of λ/4 corresponds to a phase difference of:
x: Phase difference = (2π/λ) × path difference = (2π/λ) × (λ/4) = π/2. A full wavelength of path difference corresponds to 2π.

q: Two coherent sound sources vibrate in antiphase (phase difference π). At a point that is exactly the same distance from both sources, the sound is:
o: A minimum, because the waves arrive in opposite phase
A maximum, because the path difference is zero
A maximum, because the sources are coherent
x: With zero path difference the waves keep the phase difference they started with, which is π. They arrive in opposite phase and interfere destructively.

q: For two waves to cancel completely at a point of destructive interference, they must arrive with:
o: Equal amplitudes and zero phase difference
Different amplitudes and zero phase difference
Equal amplitudes and a phase difference of π
x: Complete cancellation needs equal and opposite displacements at every instant: equal amplitudes in opposite phase. With unequal amplitudes the minimum is not zero.

q: In the laboratory, two coherent sources of sound are most easily obtained by:
o: Connecting each loudspeaker to its own signal generator
Using two tuning forks of different frequencies
Moving one loudspeaker rapidly to and fro
Connecting two loudspeakers to the same signal generator
x: Two speakers fed by one signal generator vibrate at the same frequency with a fixed phase relation, so they are coherent. Separate generators drift in phase.

q: Two loudspeakers vibrate in phase. Constructive interference occurs at points where the path difference is:
x: When the path difference is 0, λ, 2λ, ... the waves arrive in phase and reinforce each other. An odd multiple of λ/2 gives destructive interference.

q: Two in-phase sound sources produce destructive interference at points where the path difference is:
x: A path difference of λ/2, 3λ/2, 5λ/2, ... makes the waves arrive in opposite phase, so a compression meets a rarefaction and the sound is a minimum.

q: Two loudspeakers in phase emit sound of frequency 340 Hz (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). A listener is 4.0 m from one speaker and 5.5 m from the other. The listener hears:
o: A loud sound, as interference is constructive
No change, as sound waves do not interfere
A soft sound, as interference is destructive
x: λ = v/f = 340/340 = 1 m. The path difference is 1.5 m = 1.5λ, an odd multiple of λ/2, so interference is destructive.

q: Two in-phase loudspeakers emit sound of wavelength 0.5 m. The smallest path difference that gives destructive interference is:
x: Destructive interference first occurs at a path difference of λ/2 = 0.5/2 = 0.25 m. A path difference of 0.5 m (one whole λ) gives constructive interference.

q: Two in-phase loudspeakers are at distances from a point P that differ by 0.5 m. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. The lowest frequency for which P is a point of destructive interference is:
x: The lowest frequency means the longest wavelength, given by λ/2 = 0.5 m, so λ = 1 m. Then f = v/λ = 340/1 = 340 Hz.

q: At points of destructive interference of sound, the energy of the two waves is:
o: Redistributed, so more energy reaches the points of constructive interference
x: Interference does not destroy energy; it redistributes it. Less energy at the quiet points is balanced by more at the loud points, so energy is conserved.

q: A student walks along a line parallel to two loudspeakers connected to the same signal generator and hears the sound become alternately loud and soft. This is due to:
x: As the student moves, the path difference from the two coherent sources changes, giving alternate constructive (loud) and destructive (soft) interference. Sound cannot be polarised.

q: Two tuning forks of frequencies 256 Hz and 260 Hz are sounded together. The number of beats heard per second is:
x: Beat frequency = difference of the two frequencies = 260 − 256 = 4 Hz. 258 Hz is the average frequency, which is the pitch heard, not the beat rate.

q: A tuning fork of unknown frequency gives 3 beats per second with a 384 Hz fork. When the unknown fork is loaded with a little wax, the beats increase to 5 per second. The original frequency of the unknown fork was:
x: Wax lowers a fork's frequency. If it were 387 Hz, lowering it would reduce the beats; since beats increased, it must have been 384 − 3 = 381 Hz, and lowering it moves it further from 384 Hz.

q: Beats are produced by the superposition of two sound waves that have:
o: Exactly equal frequencies, travelling in opposite directions
Exactly equal frequencies and the same phase
Slightly different frequencies, travelling in the same direction
x: Two waves of slightly different frequencies go in and out of phase periodically, so the loudness rises and falls: beats. Equal frequencies in opposite directions give a stationary wave.

q: A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency and amplitude that:
o: Travel at right angles to each other
Have a constant phase difference of π/2 and travel together
x: A stationary (standing) wave arises when two identical progressive waves travel through the same medium in opposite directions, for example an incident and a reflected wave.

q: Which statement about a stationary wave is correct?
o: There is no net transfer of energy along the medium
It carries energy along the medium at the wave speed
All its particles vibrate with the same amplitude
Particles in all its segments vibrate in the same phase
x: In a stationary wave energy is stored and shuttles locally between kinetic and potential forms; there is no net flow along the medium. Amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes.

q: Two particles of a stationary wave lie in adjacent loops, one on each side of a node. The phase difference between their vibrations is:
x: All particles within one loop (between two adjacent nodes) move in phase, while particles in adjacent loops move in opposite phase, a phase difference of π.

q: How does the amplitude of the particles in a stationary wave compare with that in a progressive wave?
o: In a stationary wave it varies from zero at nodes to a maximum at antinodes; in a progressive wave it is the same for all particles
It is the same for all particles in both waves
In a progressive wave it varies from point to point; in a stationary wave it is the same for all particles
It is zero for all particles of a stationary wave
x: In a progressive wave every particle vibrates with the same amplitude. In a stationary wave the amplitude depends on position: zero at nodes, maximum at antinodes.

q: On a string fixed at both ends, the two waves that superpose to form the stationary wave are:
o: Two waves from two different vibrators at each end
A transverse wave and a longitudinal wave
The incident wave and the wave reflected from the fixed end
A wave on the string and a sound wave in the air
x: A wave sent along the string is reflected at the fixed end and travels back. The incident and reflected waves have the same frequency and amplitude and travel in opposite directions, forming a stationary wave.

q: Two progressive waves, each of amplitude 2 mm, travelling in opposite directions form a stationary wave. The amplitude of vibration at an antinode is:
x: At an antinode the two waves always arrive in phase, so the displacements add: 2 + 2 = 4 mm. Zero is the amplitude at a node.

q: Two identical waves travelling in opposite directions along a string form a stationary wave. At an instant when the two waves are in exactly opposite phase at every point, the string:
o: Has its maximum displacement at the antinodes
Has the shape of a sine wave of double amplitude
Has the shape of a sine wave of half amplitude
Is a straight line, with zero displacement everywhere
x: When the waves are in antiphase everywhere, their displacements cancel at every point, so the whole string is momentarily straight (though its particles are moving).

q: A string vibrates as a stationary wave at a frequency of 50 Hz. How many times per second does the whole string become momentarily straight?
x: All particles of a stationary wave pass through their mean positions together, twice in each cycle. So the string is straight 2 × 50 = 100 times per second.

q: In a stationary wave, the positions of the nodes and antinodes:
o: Move forward at the speed of the wave
Move backward at half the speed of the wave
Change randomly from moment to moment
x: Unlike a progressive wave, the pattern of a stationary wave does not travel: the nodes and antinodes remain at fixed positions, which is why it is called stationary.

q: A node in a stationary wave is a point where:
o: The particle moves with maximum speed
x: At a node the two waves always cancel, so the particle there stays at rest with zero displacement. Maximum amplitude occurs at an antinode.

q: In a stationary wave of wavelength λ, the distance between two adjacent nodes is:
x: Adjacent nodes, like adjacent antinodes, are half a wavelength apart. A node and its neighbouring antinode are λ/4 apart.

q: The distance between a node and the next antinode in a stationary wave of wavelength λ is:
x: Nodes are λ/2 apart and an antinode lies midway between two nodes, so a node and the adjacent antinode are λ/4 apart.

q: In a stationary wave, the distance between two consecutive nodes is 15 cm. The wavelength of the waves is:
x: Consecutive nodes are λ/2 apart, so λ = 2 × 15 = 30 cm.

q: A stationary sound wave of frequency 500 Hz has adjacent nodes 0.34 m apart. The speed of sound is:
x: λ = 2 × 0.34 = 0.68 m, so v = fλ = 500 × 0.68 = 340 m s⁻¹. 170 m s⁻¹ comes from forgetting that nodes are λ/2 apart.

q: In a stationary wave, the distance from the first node to the fourth node is 1.5 m. The wavelength is:
x: From the first to the fourth node there are 3 gaps of λ/2: 3 × λ/2 = 1.5 m, so λ = 1.0 m. Counting 4 gaps instead of 3 gives 0.75 m.

q: As a string vibrating in a stationary wave passes through its straight position, the particles with the greatest kinetic energy are those at:
o: Points midway between a node and an antinode only
x: Antinode particles have the largest amplitude, so they have the greatest speed at the mean position. Node particles are always at rest.

q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in three loops. Counting the ends, the number of nodes and antinodes is:
x: Each loop has one antinode at its centre, giving 3 antinodes. The loops are bounded by nodes, including the two fixed ends, giving 3 + 1 = 4 nodes.

q: In a stationary wave the distance between two consecutive antinodes is 20 cm. The distance between a node and the adjacent antinode is:
x: Consecutive antinodes are λ/2 = 20 cm apart, so λ = 40 cm. A node and the adjacent antinode are λ/4 = 10 cm apart.

q: A string of length L is fixed at both ends and vibrates in its fundamental mode. The wavelength of the stationary wave is:
x: In the fundamental mode there is one loop with nodes at both ends, so L = λ/2 and λ = 2L.

q: A string 0.5 m long, fixed at both ends, carries transverse waves at 200 m s⁻¹. Its fundamental frequency is:
x: f₁ = v/2L = 200/(2 × 0.5) = 200 Hz. Using v/L would give 400 Hz and v/4L would give 100 Hz.

q: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is 100 Hz. The frequency of its third harmonic is:
x: For a string, fₙ = nf₁, so the third harmonic is 3 × 100 = 300 Hz.

q: A string 1.2 m long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in four loops. The wavelength of the waves on the string is:
x: Each loop is λ/2 long: 4 × λ/2 = 1.2 m, so λ = 0.6 m. 0.3 m is the length of one loop.

q: The tension in a stretched string is made four times as large, with its length and mass per unit length unchanged. Its fundamental frequency becomes:
x: Wave speed v = √(T/m) where m is mass per unit length, and f₁ = v/2L. Four times the tension doubles v and so doubles f₁.

q: A string 0.5 m long has a mass per unit length of 0.01 kg m⁻¹ and is stretched by a tension of 100 N. Its fundamental frequency is:
x: v = √(T/m) = √(100/0.01) = √10000 = 100 m s⁻¹. f₁ = v/2L = 100/(2 × 0.5) = 100 Hz. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 200 Hz.

q: A string fixed at both ends can vibrate with frequencies:
o: Only odd multiples of the fundamental
Only even multiples of the fundamental
All integral multiples of the fundamental
x: For a string fₙ = nv/2L with n = 1, 2, 3, ..., so all harmonics, odd and even, are possible. Only odd harmonics is the rule for a pipe closed at one end.

q: The vibrating length of a stretched string is doubled while the tension is unchanged. The fundamental frequency:
x: The wave speed depends on tension and mass per unit length, which are unchanged, and f₁ = v/2L. Doubling L halves f₁.

q: A stretched string fixed at both ends has two consecutive harmonics at 300 Hz and 400 Hz. Its fundamental frequency is:
x: Consecutive harmonics of a string differ by f₁, so f₁ = 400 − 300 = 100 Hz. They are the third and fourth harmonics.

q: The fundamental frequency of a guitar string is 120 Hz. The frequency of its second overtone is:
x: The first overtone is the second harmonic and the second overtone is the third harmonic: 3 × 120 = 360 Hz. 240 Hz is the first overtone.

q: In an organ pipe closed at one end, the closed end and the open end are respectively:
o: A displacement antinode and a displacement node
A displacement node and a displacement antinode
x: Air cannot move at the closed end, so it is a displacement node. Air moves freely at the open end, which is a displacement antinode.

q: A pipe closed at one end can produce:
o: Only odd harmonics of its fundamental
Only even harmonics of its fundamental
x: With a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, L must be an odd number of quarter wavelengths, so fₙ = nv/4L with n = 1, 3, 5, ... only.

q: A pipe 0.25 m long is closed at one end. Neglecting end correction, the wavelength of its fundamental note is:
x: In the fundamental of a closed pipe the length is λ/4, so λ = 4 × 0.25 = 1.0 m. 0.5 m would be the answer for an open pipe.

q: A pipe 0.5 m long is open at both ends. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Neglecting end correction, its fundamental frequency is:
x: For an open pipe f₁ = v/2L = 340/(2 × 0.5) = 340 Hz. 170 Hz would be the fundamental of a closed pipe of the same length.

q: A pipe 0.5 m long is closed at one end. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Neglecting end correction, its fundamental frequency is:
x: For a closed pipe f₁ = v/4L = 340/(4 × 0.5) = 170 Hz. 340 Hz would be the open-pipe value.

q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 100 Hz. Which of the following frequencies can it NOT produce?
x: A closed pipe produces only odd harmonics: 100, 300, 500, 700 Hz, ... 200 Hz is the second harmonic, which is missing.

q: Two pipes have the same length; one is open at both ends and the other is closed at one end. The ratio of the fundamental frequency of the open pipe to that of the closed pipe is:
x: f(open) = v/2L and f(closed) = v/4L, so the ratio is (v/2L) : (v/4L) = 2 : 1.

q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 150 Hz. The next higher frequency it can produce is:
x: A closed pipe gives only odd harmonics, so after 150 Hz comes the third harmonic, 3 × 150 = 450 Hz. 300 Hz would be the next one for an open pipe.

q: In a pipe open at both ends sounding its fundamental note, there is:
o: A node at each end and one antinode at the centre
A node at one end and an antinode at the other
An antinode at each end and one node at the centre
Two nodes inside the pipe and antinodes at the ends
x: Both open ends are displacement antinodes, and the simplest pattern between them has one node in the middle, so L = λ/2.

q: A pipe open at both ends has a fundamental frequency of 300 Hz. If one end is now closed, the new fundamental frequency is (neglect end correction):
x: Open: f = v/2L = 300 Hz. Closed: f = v/4L, which is half of v/2L, so the new fundamental is 150 Hz.

q: The principle of superposition states that when two or more waves overlap at a point, the resultant displacement is:
o: The product of the individual displacements
The vector sum of the individual displacements
Always equal to the larger displacement
x: By the principle of superposition, the resultant displacement at any instant is the vector (algebraic, with signs) sum of the displacements due to each wave.

q: On a rope, a pulse of displacement +3 cm and a pulse of displacement −1 cm overlap at the same point. The resultant displacement at that point is:
x: Displacements add with their signs: (+3) + (−1) = +2 cm. +4 cm comes from ignoring the sign of the inverted pulse.

q: Two pulses travelling in opposite directions on a rope pass through each other. After they have passed:
o: Each pulse continues with its original shape and speed
The pulses join into one larger pulse
x: Waves pass through one another without being permanently changed. They combine only while overlapping, then continue as before.

q: Two pulses of the same shape and size, one upright and one inverted, travel towards each other on a rope. At the instant they exactly overlap, the rope is flat. At that instant the energy in that part of the rope is:
o: Zero, because the displacement is zero
Entirely kinetic, because the rope particles are moving
Entirely potential, because the rope is stretched
x: The displacements cancel, so the rope is momentarily flat and unstretched, but its particles are still moving. The energy has not disappeared; at that instant it is all kinetic.

q: Noise-cancelling headphones reduce unwanted sound by producing a sound wave that, compared with the noise, has:
o: Double the frequency and the same phase
The same frequency and amplitude but opposite phase
The same frequency and phase but double the amplitude
A much higher frequency and the same amplitude
x: A wave equal in frequency and amplitude but in opposite phase superposes destructively with the noise, cancelling it.

q: Which statement about the superposition of two waves is correct?
o: The resultant displacement can be smaller than either individual displacement
The resultant amplitude is always the sum of the two amplitudes
The waves bounce off each other when they meet
Superposition applies only to sound waves
x: When the displacements have opposite signs, their sum can be smaller than either one, even zero. The amplitudes add only when the waves are in phase.

q: The principle of superposition applies to:
o: All waves, both mechanical and electromagnetic
x: Superposition is a general property of waves. It explains interference of sound and of light, and stationary waves on strings and in pipes.

q: Interference, beats and stationary waves are all explained by:
x: Each arises from adding the displacements of overlapping waves: coherent waves give interference, slightly different frequencies give beats, and opposite-travelling waves give stationary waves.

q: Two coherent waves of amplitudes 6 mm and 2 mm superpose at different points with different phase differences. The resultant amplitude can have any value from:
x: The maximum, in phase, is 6 + 2 = 8 mm; the minimum, in opposite phase, is 6 − 2 = 4 mm. Zero is possible only when the amplitudes are equal.

q: A body moves with simple harmonic motion. Its acceleration is:
o: Proportional to its displacement and directed away from the mean position
Proportional to its displacement and directed towards the mean position
x: SHM is defined by a = −ω²x: acceleration proportional to displacement from the mean position and always directed towards it, as the minus sign shows.

q: A particle in SHM has angular frequency 10 rad s⁻¹. When its displacement is 0.02 m, the magnitude of its acceleration is:
x: a = ω²x = 10² × 0.02 = 100 × 0.02 = 2 m s⁻², directed towards the mean position. 0.2 m s⁻² comes from using ω instead of ω².

q: A mass of 0.4 kg hangs on a spring of spring constant 40 N m⁻¹ and oscillates vertically. Its time period is:
A simple pendulum is 2.5 m long. Taking g = 10 m s⁻², its time period is:
The mass of the bob of a simple pendulum is doubled and its length is made four times as long. Its time period becomes:
x: T = 2π√(l/g) does not depend on the mass of the bob. Four times the length gives √4 = 2 times the period.

q: At an extreme position of a body in SHM:
o: Its velocity is maximum and its acceleration is zero
Both velocity and acceleration are zero
Both velocity and acceleration are maximum
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is maximum
x: At the extremes the body momentarily stops, and since a = −ω²x with x at its largest, the acceleration is maximum. At the mean position the reverse is true.

q: A mass on a spring oscillates in SHM with amplitude x₀. When its displacement is x₀/2, its kinetic energy is what fraction of its total energy?
x: Potential energy = ½kx² = ½k(x₀/2)² = ¼ of the total ½kx₀². Kinetic energy is the rest: 1 − ¼ = ¾ of the total.

q: The amplitude of a mass–spring oscillator is doubled. Its total energy becomes:
x: Total energy of SHM = ½kx₀², proportional to the square of the amplitude, so doubling the amplitude makes it 2² = 4 times.

q: A particle performs SHM with amplitude 0.05 m and angular frequency 20 rad s⁻¹. Its maximum speed is:
x: Maximum speed, at the mean position, is v₀ = ωx₀ = 20 × 0.05 = 1 m s⁻¹. 20 m s⁻¹ would be the maximum acceleration, ω²x₀.

q: A simple pendulum and a mass–spring oscillator both have a period of 1 s on Earth. On the Moon, where g is smaller:
o: The mass–spring period increases but the pendulum's period stays the same
The pendulum's period increases but the mass–spring period stays the same
x: T = 2π√(l/g) increases when g decreases. T = 2π√(m/k) does not involve g, so the mass–spring period is unchanged.

q: A point moves with uniform speed around a circle. The motion of its projection (foot of the perpendicular) on a diameter of the circle is:
o: Uniform motion in a straight line
x: As the point goes round, its projection moves to and fro along the diameter with acceleration proportional to its distance from the centre, directed towards the centre: this is SHM.

q: When the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter is used to describe SHM, the amplitude of the SHM is equal to:
o: Half the radius of the circle
x: The projection moves from the centre to either end of the diameter, a distance equal to the radius. So the amplitude x₀ equals the radius.

q: A point moves round a circle of radius 0.1 m at 5 revolutions per second. Its projection on a diameter performs SHM of:
x: The amplitude equals the radius, 0.1 m, and the projection completes one oscillation for each revolution, so its frequency is 5 Hz. 0.2 m is the whole length of the path.

q: A reference point moves round a circle of radius x₀ with angular velocity ω, starting at an end of the diameter on which it is projected. After time t, the displacement of its projection from the centre is:
x: After time t the radius has turned through θ = ωt, and the projection on the diameter is x = x₀ cos θ = x₀ cos ωt.

q: A point moves round a circle of radius 0.2 m with angular velocity 5 rad s⁻¹. The maximum speed of its projection on a diameter is:
x: At the centre the point's velocity is parallel to the diameter, so the projection moves with the full speed v = rω = 0.2 × 5 = 1 m s⁻¹.

q: The velocity of the projection of a uniformly rotating point is zero when the projection is at an end of the diameter because there:
o: The velocity of the rotating point is perpendicular to the diameter
The radius is parallel to the velocity
x: At the ends of the diameter the rotating point moves at right angles to the diameter, so its velocity has no component along it and the projection is momentarily at rest.

q: For a point in uniform circular motion of angular velocity ω, the acceleration of its projection on a diameter, at displacement x from the centre, is:
o: ω²x, directed away from the centre
x: The point has centripetal acceleration ω²r towards the centre. Its component along the diameter is ω²r cos θ = ω²x, directed towards the centre, which is the condition a = −ω²x for SHM.

q: The projection of a uniformly rotating point performs SHM of amplitude 5 cm and angular frequency 2 rad s⁻¹. Its speed when it is 3 cm from the centre is:
x: v = ω√(x₀² − x²) = 2√(25 − 9) = 2 × 4 = 8 cm s⁻¹. 10 cm s⁻¹ is the maximum speed ωx₀, reached only at the centre.

q: A reference point takes 0.8 s for one revolution. The time taken by its projection to move from one end of the diameter to the other is:
x: One revolution is one complete oscillation of the projection, end to end and back. Going from one end to the other is half an oscillation: 0.8/2 = 0.4 s.
